questions.q: Define glycemic index (GI) and state its significance in diabetic meal planning.
questions.a: Glycemic index ranks carbohydrate foods on a scale 0-100 based on their blood glucose response relative to glucose (GI=100). Significance: Low GI foods (≤55) produce slower, lower glucose peaks, improving postprandial control and reducing insulin demand. A wrong answer like "GI measures sugar content" reveals confusion between carbohydrate quantity and quality — students often think low-sugar foods automatically have low GI, but watermelon (GI 72) has less sugar per 100g than apple (GI 36).

questions.q: A 60 kg, 45-year-old woman with Type 2 diabetes requires 1800 kcal/day. Using 55% carbohydrate calories, calculate her daily carbohydrate allowance in grams and exchange units (1 exchange = 15g carb).
questions.a: Carb calories = 1800 × 0.55 = 990 kcal. Carb grams = 990 ÷ 4 = 247.5g ≈ 248g. Exchanges = 248 ÷ 15 = 16.5 exchanges. A wrong answer of "55 exchanges" shows student used percentage directly without converting calories to grams — classic error of skipping the 4 kcal/g conversion step. Another error: using 1800 × 0.55 ÷ 15 = 66 exchanges (forgetting 4 kcal/g).

questions.q: Design a 1600 kcal diabetic menu distributing 13 carbohydrate exchanges across 3 main meals + 2 snacks. Show exchange distribution per meal and justify timing for a patient on metformin (peak action 2-3 hours post-dose).
questions.a: Total 13 exchanges: Breakfast 4, Mid-morning 1, Lunch 4, Evening 1, Dinner 3. Timing: Metformin taken with breakfast and dinner — snacks at 2-3 hour post-dose align with peak glucose-lowering effect to prevent hypoglycemia. A wrong distribution like Breakfast 6, Lunch 4, Dinner 3 (no snacks) risks hypoglycemia during metformin peak; student misses medication-meal synchronization concept.

questions.q: Compare and contrast dietary modifications for Type 1 vs Type 2 diabetes regarding carbohydrate consistency, weight management, and hypoglycemia prevention.
questions.a: Type 1: Carbohydrate consistency critical for fixed insulin doses; weight management secondary; hypoglycemia prevention via snack timing and carb matching. Type 2: Carbohydrate distribution important but weight loss primary (calorie restriction); hypoglycemia risk lower unless on insulin/sulfonylureas. Wrong answer "Both need same carb restriction" ignores that Type 2 focuses on calorie deficit for insulin sensitivity, while Type 1 focuses on carb-insulin matching.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Diabetic patients should avoid all fruits because they contain natural sugars." Provide evidence-based counterargument with 3 specific fruit examples and their GI values.
questions.a: Statement is false. Fruits provide fiber, antioxidants, micronutrients. Low GI fruits suitable: Apple (GI 36), Orange (GI 43), Guava (GI 12). Portion control matters — 1 exchange (15g carb) = 1 small apple/100g. Wrong agreement shows "sugar avoidance" misconception — students equate all sugars as harmful, ignoring food matrix effects and nutrient density.

questions.q: Create a patient education handout (5 bullet points) explaining "carbohydrate exchange system" to a newly diagnosed diabetic with low literacy. Use analogies, avoid technical terms.
questions.a: Good answer: "Think of carb exchanges like currency notes — each 'note' = 15g carb. Your daily budget = X notes. Spend them across meals. 1 roti = 1 note, 1 katori rice = 2 notes, 1 apple = 1 note. Swap notes but don't overspend." Poor answer uses jargon like "macronutrient distribution" — reveals inability to translate clinical concepts for patient communication.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Therapeutic diet for diabetes mellitus is a ______ planned meal pattern that modifies macronutrient distribution (carbohydrates 50-55%, proteins 15-20%, fats 25-30% of total calories), emphasizes low glycemic index foods, distributes carbohydrates evenly across meals, and incorporates high-fiber sources to achieve glycemic control while meeting nutritional requirements for age, weight, activity level, and comorbid conditions.
Fill in the blank: Imagine your 55-year-old uncle just ______ with Type 2 diabetes — fasting glucose 145 mg/dL, HbA1c 8.2%, BMI 28, sedentary job.
What is Therapeutic diet for diabetes mellitus? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Therapeutic diet for diabetes mellitus is a scientifically planned meal pattern that modifies macronutrient distribution (carbohydrates 50-55%, proteins 15-20%, fats 25-30% of total calories), emphasizes low glycemic index foods, distributes carbohydrates evenly across meals, and incorporates high-fiber sources to achieve glycemic.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Therapeutic diet for diabetes mellitus?
questions.a: Students believe "diabetic diet = sugar-free diet" and recommend artificial sweeteners freely.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can calculate individualized calorie and macronutrient targets for a diabetic patient, design a day's menu with carbohydrate distribution across 5-6 meals using exchange lists, and justify food selections based on glycemic index and fiber content.
